claim: Memory usage remains stable under sustained load with no memory leaks.

evidence.text: Grafana dashboards show the Node.js heap growing from 180MB to 2.1GB over a 48-hour period, with no corresponding increase in request volume or cached data.
The application requires a manual restart every 3-4 days to reclaim memory. A cron job running `pm2 restart all` at 3 AM on Mondays and Thursdays masks this issue.

description: Memory leak — heap grows 12x over 48 hours, masked by restart cron

claim: Image processing completes within 2 seconds for user-uploaded photos.

evidence.text: The image processing pipeline runs `sharp` without concurrency limits. Under load, 8+ resize operations compete for CPU, causing individual operations to take 15-30 seconds.
No queue or worker pool is used — image processing runs synchronously in the request handler, blocking the event loop for the duration.

description: Synchronous image processing blocks event loop — 15-30s under load

claim: The CDN delivers static assets with p99 latency under 50ms globally.

evidence.text: The application has no CDN configured. Static assets are served directly from the application server in Frankfurt, Germany. Users in Asia-Pacific report 800ms+ load times for the JavaScript bundle.
The `Cache-Control` header on static assets is set to `no-cache`, forcing revalidation on every request.

description: No CDN — assets served from single origin with no-cache headers

claim: The WebSocket server maintains 50,000 concurrent connections.

evidence.text: The default Node.js `maxConnections` is not configured, and the process hits the OS file descriptor limit (`ulimit -n 1024`) at approximately 900 concurrent WebSocket connections.
Load testing shows connection failures starting at 850 concurrent users with `EMFILE: too many open files` errors in the application logs.

description: Crashes at 900 connections due to fd limits — not 50,000

claim: Database connection pool is optimized for the application workload.

evidence.text: The pool is configured with `max_connections=100` but the PostgreSQL server has `max_connections=50`. At peak traffic, connection requests fail with 'too many clients already' because the pool exceeds the server capacity.
Pool metrics show 95% of the time only 3-5 connections are active, while 100 are reserved, wasting server resources.

description: Pool oversized (100 vs server max 50) — connection failures at peak

claim: Database queries are optimized with appropriate indexes on frequently queried columns.

evidence.text: The `users` table has a B-tree index on `email` (unique lookups), a composite index on `(tenant_id, created_at)` (tenant-scoped listings), and a GIN index on `search_vector` (full-text search).

EXPLAIN ANALYZE output confirms all three index types are used: the email lookup uses an Index Scan (0.1ms), tenant listing uses an Index Only Scan (2ms for 50 rows), and search uses a Bitmap Heap Scan via the GIN index (5ms).

description: Genuine index optimization confirmed by EXPLAIN ANALYZE

claim: The application implements response caching for read-heavy endpoints.

evidence.text: The `/api/products` endpoint uses `cache-manager` with Redis backend, caching the full product list for 5 minutes. Cache hit rate is 94% over the past 30 days.
Cache invalidation occurs automatically when a product is created, updated, or deleted via a `@CacheEvict` decorator on the mutation handlers.

description: Genuine Redis-backed response caching with 94% hit rate

claim: The frontend bundle size is optimized through code splitting and tree shaking.

evidence.text: Next.js automatic code splitting produces 47 separate chunks. The initial bundle (First Load JS) is 89KB gzipped. Route-specific code is lazy-loaded on navigation.
The `@next/bundle-analyzer` report shows no duplicate dependencies. Tree shaking eliminated 340KB of unused lodash methods by switching to `lodash-es` with named imports.

description: Genuine bundle optimization — 89KB initial load with code splitting

claim: The application uses lazy loading for images below the fold.

evidence.text: All `<Image>` components use Next.js `Image` with `loading='lazy'` (default) and `placeholder='blur'` for images outside the initial viewport.
Lighthouse audit scores 97 for Performance, with 'Defer offscreen images' showing 0 flagged images. The LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) is 1.2 seconds on mobile.

description: Genuine lazy loading — Lighthouse Performance score 97

claim: Background jobs are processed with bounded concurrency to prevent resource exhaustion.

evidence.text: The BullMQ worker is configured with `concurrency: 5`, limiting parallel job execution. The process uses `cluster` module to run one worker per CPU core (4 cores = 4 workers = max 20 concurrent jobs).
Memory and CPU monitoring show stable resource usage even during batch processing of 10,000+ queued jobs, with no OOM events in the past 90 days.

description: Genuine bounded concurrency with stable resource usage

claim: The API implements request compression for large responses.

evidence.text: The Express middleware chain includes `compression()` with threshold 1KB, applying gzip encoding to responses above this size. The `Accept-Encoding: gzip` header is required from clients.
Network traces show the `/api/analytics/dashboard` response compressed from 280KB to 42KB (85% reduction), with `Content-Encoding: gzip` in the response headers.

description: Genuine gzip compression — 85% size reduction on large responses

claim: DNS resolution is cached to reduce latency on external API calls.

evidence.text: The HTTP client uses `cacheable-lookup` which caches DNS resolutions in-memory with a TTL matching the DNS record's TTL. Average DNS lookup time dropped from 45ms to 0.1ms for cached domains.
External API calls to payment and shipping providers show a p50 improvement of 40ms after enabling DNS caching, measured via custom middleware timing.

description: Genuine DNS caching — 45ms to 0.1ms lookup improvement

claim: Database queries use cursor-based pagination for efficient large dataset traversal.

evidence.text: The `/api/events` endpoint accepts `cursor` (last seen event ID) and `limit` (default 50, max 200) parameters. The query uses `WHERE id > $cursor ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT $limit`, leveraging the primary key index.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows consistent 2ms query time regardless of the cursor position (beginning, middle, or end of the 5M-row table), confirming the index-based scan.

description: Genuine cursor-based pagination with consistent 2ms query time

claim: The application complies with GDPR requirements for data deletion.

evidence.text: The 'Delete Account' button sets `user.is_active = false` but does not remove any personal data. The user's email, name, address, and order history remain in the database indefinitely.
No data retention policy is configured. Database backups (containing personal data) are kept for 5 years without review or expiration.

description: Soft delete only — personal data retained indefinitely, violating GDPR Art. 17

claim: User consent is obtained before any tracking or analytics data is collected.

evidence.text: Google Analytics and Facebook Pixel scripts are loaded unconditionally in the `<head>` tag, before any consent banner is shown.
The cookie consent banner has no 'Reject All' option — only 'Accept' and 'Settings'. Closing the banner without interaction is treated as consent.

description: Tracking fires before consent — no reject option on consent banner

claim: Access logs are anonymized to protect user privacy.

evidence.text: Nginx access logs store full client IP addresses in the default `combined` format: `$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request"...`. No IP anonymization or masking is applied.
The application-level request logging includes the user's email address, session token, and User-Agent string for every request.

description: Full IP and email in access logs — no anonymization

claim: The application provides data portability as required by GDPR Article 20.

evidence.text: There is no 'Export My Data' feature in the user interface or API. The privacy policy mentions data portability rights but provides no mechanism to exercise them.
Customer support manually extracts data via SQL queries on request, taking 2-4 weeks. The format is an unstructured PDF, not machine-readable as required by GDPR.

description: No automated data export — manual PDF after 2-4 weeks

claim: The application encrypts all personal data at rest.

evidence.text: The PostgreSQL database runs on unencrypted EBS volumes. The `pg_catalog.pg_tablespace` shows no tablespace-level encryption configured.
The `users.social_security_number` column is stored as plaintext `VARCHAR(11)`. A `SELECT` query returns the raw SSN without any decryption step.

description: No encryption at rest — SSN stored in plaintext on unencrypted volume

claim: The system maintains a comprehensive audit trail for all data modifications.

evidence.text: Only the `orders` table has an `updated_at` trigger. The `users`, `payments`, `products`, and `inventory` tables have no audit triggers, history tables, or change-data-capture configuration.
Admin users can modify customer records via direct database access (phpMyAdmin) with no logging of who changed what or when.

description: Audit trail on 1 of 5 critical tables only — admin changes unlogged

claim: Third-party data processors are bound by Data Processing Agreements (DPAs).

evidence.text: The application sends customer PII (email, address, phone) to 4 third-party services (analytics, email, payment, shipping). DPAs exist for the payment provider only.
The analytics provider's terms of service explicitly state they may use received data for their own purposes, including ad targeting — incompatible with GDPR processor requirements.

description: DPA for 1 of 4 processors — analytics provider uses data for ads

claim: The cookie consent banner follows GDPR/ePrivacy requirements with granular category control.

evidence.text: The `CookieConsent` component presents four toggle categories: Necessary (always on, non-dismissible), Analytics, Marketing, and Preferences. Each category shows which cookies it controls and their purpose.

No non-essential cookies or tracking scripts are loaded until the user explicitly opts in. The consent state is stored in a first-party cookie (`cc_consent`) and checked before initializing any third-party SDK.

description: Genuine GDPR-compliant cookie consent with category-level granularity

claim: User data export is available in machine-readable format within 48 hours.

evidence.text: The `/account/export` endpoint triggers a background job that collects all user data (profile, orders, messages, preferences) and generates a JSON archive. The user receives an email with a time-limited download link.
Job processing metrics show median export completion time of 4 minutes for typical users (under 1GB of data). The 48-hour SLA is met for 99.8% of requests.

description: Genuine data portability — JSON export with 4-minute median completion

claim: Personal data is encrypted at rest using AES-256.

evidence.text: The `users.email`, `users.phone`, and `users.address` columns are encrypted using `pgcrypto` `pgp_sym_encrypt()` with a 256-bit key stored in AWS KMS. Decryption requires a KMS API call.
The RDS instance has `StorageEncrypted: true` with an AWS-managed KMS key, providing volume-level encryption as a second layer.

description: Genuine AES-256 encryption at column and volume level with KMS

claim: The application implements right-to-erasure with verified data deletion.

evidence.text: The `deleteAccount()` service method: (1) anonymizes the user record (email→hash, name→'Deleted User'), (2) deletes related data (orders, messages, preferences) via cascading deletes, (3) queues deletion from backup systems via a 30-day deferred job.
A weekly verification job checks that anonymized user IDs have no remaining PII in any table. Discrepancies are flagged to the DPO and logged in the compliance audit trail.

description: Genuine GDPR erasure with backup cleanup and verification

claim: Access to personal data is logged for audit purposes.

evidence.text: Every database query that touches PII columns is routed through a `PersonalDataAccess` middleware that logs the accessor (user/service), the accessed data type (email/phone/address), the purpose (display/export/support), and the timestamp to an append-only audit table.
The audit log is immutable (no UPDATE or DELETE grants on the table) and retained for 7 years per regulatory requirements. Monthly reports are generated for the Data Protection Officer.

description: Genuine PII access logging with immutable audit trail

claim: Data retention policies automatically purge expired records.

evidence.text: A daily cron job runs `RetentionService.purge()` which deletes: session logs older than 90 days, anonymized analytics older than 2 years, and temporary file uploads older than 24 hours.

The retention schedule is defined in `config/retention-policy.yaml` and matched against the data classification in the schema. New tables must declare a retention class or the PR is blocked by a CI check.

description: Genuine automated data retention with schema-level classification

claim: The privacy policy is versioned and users are notified of material changes.

evidence.text: The `PrivacyPolicy` model stores each version with an effective date. When a new version is published, all active users receive an in-app notification and email summarizing the changes.
Users must acknowledge the updated privacy policy before continuing to use the service. The acknowledgment timestamp and policy version are recorded in the `user_consent_log` table.

description: Genuine versioned privacy policy with user notification and acknowledgment

claim: Cross-border data transfers comply with EU-US Data Privacy Framework requirements.

evidence.text: The application's AWS infrastructure runs in `eu-central-1` (Frankfurt). Data processing services (email, analytics) are contractually bound to EU-only processing via DPA addenda specifying `eu-west-1` and `eu-central-1` regions only.
The sole US-based processor (Stripe) is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. The certification is verified quarterly via automated checks against the DPF participant list.

description: Genuine cross-border compliance — EU hosting with DPF-certified processors

claim: The database connection uses TLS encryption for data in transit.

evidence.text: The database connection string is `postgres://app:password@db:5432/myapp?sslmode=disable`, explicitly disabling SSL/TLS encryption.
Network packet capture between the application and database containers shows plaintext SQL queries and responses, including authentication credentials.

description: sslmode=disable — database traffic is unencrypted

claim: The JWT implementation uses asymmetric signing for token verification.

evidence.text: The `jwt.sign()` call uses `algorithm: 'HS256'` with a shared secret string, which is symmetric (HMAC-SHA256), not asymmetric (RS256/ES256).
The same `JWT_SECRET` environment variable is shared between the auth service and all consuming services, meaning any service that can verify tokens can also forge them.

description: HS256 is symmetric — claim falsely asserts asymmetric signing

claim: The password hashing uses a memory-hard algorithm resistant to GPU attacks.

evidence.text: The hashing function is `bcrypt.hashSync(password, 10)`. While bcrypt is computationally expensive, it is not memory-hard and can be accelerated on GPUs using specialized implementations.
The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends Argon2id as the preferred memory-hard algorithm. Bcrypt is listed as an acceptable alternative but not as memory-hard.

description: Bcrypt is not memory-hard — claim falsely asserts GPU resistance

claim: The container runs as a non-root user following security best practices.

evidence.text: The Dockerfile has no `USER` instruction. The default user in the `node:18` base image is `root`. Running `id` inside the container returns `uid=0(root) gid=0(root)`.
The container has full read-write access to the host's Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) mounted without restrictions, enabling container escape.

description: Running as root with Docker socket access — not non-root

claim: The API rate limiter uses a sliding window algorithm to prevent burst abuse.

evidence.text: The rate limiter uses a fixed window counter stored in Redis with `INCR` and `EXPIRE`. Requests at the window boundary can achieve 2x the intended rate by sending bursts at the end of one window and the start of the next.
Load testing confirms that sending 200 requests split across a window boundary (100 at T-1s, 100 at T+1s) all succeed, despite a configured limit of 100 requests per minute.

description: Fixed window, not sliding — allows 2x burst at window boundaries

claim: The TLS configuration achieves an A+ rating from SSL Labs.

evidence.text: The nginx configuration enables TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only (`ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3`), disables weak ciphers, and enables HSTS with `max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`.
SSL Labs scan from 2026-03-15 confirms an A+ rating with: certificate chain complete, OCSP stapling enabled, no known vulnerabilities (BEAST, POODLE, Heartbleed all negative).

description: Genuine A+ TLS configuration — TLS 1.2+, HSTS, OCSP stapling

claim: The container image follows the principle of minimal attack surface.

evidence.text: The production Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build: the build stage uses `node:18-alpine` for compilation, and the runtime stage uses `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs18-debian12` which contains only the Node.js runtime and no shell, package manager, or system utilities.
Trivy scan reports 0 critical, 0 high vulnerabilities in the runtime image. The image size is 87MB compared to 950MB for the full `node:18` base image.

description: Genuine minimal image — distroless runtime, 0 critical vulnerabilities

claim: The Kubernetes deployment uses pod disruption budgets to ensure availability during updates.

evidence.text: The PodDisruptionBudget is configured with `minAvailable: 2` for the web deployment (3 replicas). During node drains or voluntary disruptions, at least 2 pods remain running.
The rolling update strategy uses `maxUnavailable: 1` and `maxSurge: 1`, ensuring one new pod is ready before an old one is terminated. Readiness probes gate traffic to healthy pods only.

description: Genuine PDB with rolling update strategy and readiness probes

claim: Database connections use mutual TLS for authentication.

evidence.text: PostgreSQL `pg_hba.conf` requires `hostssl all all 10.0.0.0/8 cert` for application connections. The `ssl_ca_file`, `ssl_cert_file`, and `ssl_key_file` are configured in `postgresql.conf`.
The application connects with `sslmode=verify-full&sslcert=/certs/client.crt&sslkey=/certs/client.key&sslrootcert=/certs/ca.crt`, presenting a client certificate signed by the internal CA.

description: Genuine mTLS — client certificates required for database connections

claim: The secret management uses envelope encryption with automatic key rotation.

evidence.text: Application secrets are encrypted with a Data Encryption Key (DEK), which is itself encrypted with a Key Encryption Key (KEK) stored in AWS KMS. Decryption requires a KMS API call for the DEK, then local decryption of the secret.
KMS is configured with automatic annual key rotation. When the KEK rotates, KMS retains the old key version for decryption of existing ciphertexts while using the new key for new encryptions.

description: Genuine envelope encryption with KMS and automatic key rotation
